newsitem.title: UK: UK markets comforted by Tory unity, tax prudence.
newsitem.headline: UK markets comforted by Tory unity, tax prudence.

text.p: British financial markets took some comfort on Friday from signs of unity at the traditionally pro-business ruling Conservative Party's annual conference and indications that a give-away budget is not on the agenda.

The conference went more smoothly than it might have, with the lid kept firmly on simmering divisions over Europe. But with opinion polls suggesting the opposition Labour Party is poised to take power, the markets were less than agog.
"The potential was for the conference to be a disaster for the Tories with the split over Europe and the sleaze headlines," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
In the run-up to this week's conference in Bournemouth, the British press had been awash with stories of politicians taking cash to ask parliamentary questions.

"The big unanswered question is whether this new-found unity will last past the weekend," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "But the conference as a whole has gone much better than anyone expected."

United or not, unless the Conservatives' fortunes improve dramatically -- most opinion polls show Labour at least 20 points ahead -- the markets will be far more interested in Labour's line on a single European currency.
But the British budget, due on November 26, will get them sitting up and taking notice. And there, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke provided some reassurance this week.
In his speech on Thursday, he said taxes would only be cut if affordable and sustainable -- partly a pre-budget ploy to deflate expectations, but analysts said it had a ring of truth.

"What he is going to argue on Budget day is that some tax reductions now are sustainable because he is able to cut public spending and keep public spending down over the medium term," said Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs.
In its "Green Budget", produced in conjunction with the Institute for Fiscal Studies, Goldman Sachs forecast tax cuts of around three billion pounds ($4.72 billion) would be unveiled.
"That's probably about on the mark," Shepperd said.

With Britain's public sector deficit proving tough to rein in -- the UK Treasury has already raised its Public Sector Borrowing Requirement forecast from 22.5 billion pounds to 27 billion for this year -- and consumer spending gathering pace, the markets would probably prefer no tax cuts.
"But let's get real," Shepperd said. "It's a pre-election budget. Tax cuts will come as no surprise to anyone."
Analysts said the united front put up by the Tories this week meant Britain's markets had one less thing to worry about.

Minister after minister took to the platform to espouse to the government's wait-and-see policy over a single European currency. And delegates were sent home with Prime Minister John Major's assertion that ever-closer integration with Europe was not desirable, ringing in their ears.

"But it hasn't had much impact on the City," Shepperd said. "The Tories have tried hard to present a united front but the markets are far more interested in what the Labour Party has to say about Europe."

So a veneer of unity over Europe hardly got City screens buzzing. In fact, the markets were far more shaken by figures, released on Thursday, showing underlying UK inflation edged up to 2.9 percent year-on-year in September.

Gilt futures tumbled nearly a point after the inflation figures on Thursday before steadying on Friday. The pound shot higher against the mark and the FTSE-100 index of leading British shares hovered around the 4,000 level, little changed.
But economists said that Clarke's performance was a brave one and had been lapped up for its style, if not content.
"Clarke's performance was superb, some terrific one-liners," Shepperd said. "He didn't say much, but he said it very well."
Most analysts found it hard to say the same about Major's closing speech. "It looks great for now but can it last. It's by no means certain that it can," Coleman said.
